Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Margaret Vance had never imagined that standing helpless in a checkout line would permanently fracture her sense of safety. Three years ago, during an ordinary trip with her husband, David, his chest had seized mid-stride, the grocery bags scattering across the tile as his breathing grew ragged. In the chaotic aftermath, some moments remained terrifyingly sharp—the exact pattern of the ceiling tiles, the metallic click of the automatic doors, the way David’s eyes had searched hers for reassurance—while other stretches of those frantic hours sat in a void so complete she could not account for a single second of time. When the emergency physician later confirmed that David’s heart had stopped despite her presence, Margaret’s conviction that she had failed to protect him took root. She was certain the event happened because of the way she had acted, a self-reproach that quickly eroded her faith in her own judgment. She no longer trusted herself to read a room, to gauge risk, or to navigate crisis, and that profound doubt became the lens through which she viewed every memory of that day. Because she was convinced her past choices had been fatally flawed, Margaret’s daily life began to contract around her negative appraisals. She stopped walking past the memorial plaque outside the hospital, rerouting her convent deliveries through side streets rather than facing the site where David had fallen. She also began performing silent mental rituals the moment any object, sound, or phrase reminded her of him, a quiet litany of protective counters she believed would keep further catastrophe at bay. These avoidance strategies and magical prevention attempts were not born of fear alone; they were direct consequences of her belief that she lacked the competence to survive loss without spiraling into ruin. Simultaneously, her conviction that she had been powerless in that moment actively shaped how the past intruded upon her present. The guilt she carried made the memories of the event feel less like historical records and more like immediate, unprocessed threats, each recollection sharpened by the relentless pressure of her own self-blame until the past felt permanently alive. The memories, however, would not be contained by her routines. When the scent of formaldehyde drifted from the parish clinic or the heavy oak doors of the convent infirmary swung open, Margaret’s composure fractured; the vivid details of David’s collapse would flood back without warning, bypassing her defenses entirely. Faced with the sheer force of these intrusions, she retreated further into her maladaptive strategies, locking herself in the scriptorium or spending hours meticulously cleaning the same altar cloth to keep the past physically distant. Yet this retreat only deepened her distress. Her reliance on mental rituals and site avoidance did not quiet the memories; instead, the very effort to suppress them acted as a cognitive alarm, ensuring that any fleeting memory of David remained hyper-aroused and impossible to dismiss. The memories continued to intrude, and the mental prayers she performed to ward them off only heightened her awareness of what she had lost, trapping her in a relentless feedback loop. By constantly fleeing the very thoughts that demanded processing, Margaret inadvertently reinforced her original terror. Her avoidance became a silent admission that she was fundamentally unsafe in her own mind, which in turn fed directly back into her conviction that she could not rely on herself to navigate daily life. The mental rituals meant to protect her only validated her belief that she was too fragile to cope, which in turn intensified the self-blame that fueled the original appraisals. When the convent infirmary began requiring her to lead morning rounds along the main thoroughfare, the pressure became unbearable. She sought counseling not to abandon her faith, but to break the cycle that had convinced her she was incapable of survival. Margaret now sits in the therapist’s office, hoping to reclaim a sense of competence that feels long gone, terrified that without her rituals, she will once again be the woman who stood helpless while her husband slipped away.
